h1: American and Canadian rye whisky compared
title: American vs Canadian Rye Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: How American rye and Canadian rye whisky differ: the legal rules, the grain content, the casks and what each tends to taste like.
teaser: Both are called rye. Only one of them has to contain much rye.
standfirst: Rye whisky means something precise in the United States and something much looser in Canada. Knowing the difference saves you from buying a soft Canadian blend when you wanted a spicy American rye, or the other way round.
sections: American rye has a legal recipe

In the United States, rye whisky must be made from a mash of at least 51% rye. The rest of the rules mirror bourbon: distilled to no more than 80% ABV, filled at no more than 62.5% ABV into new charred oak containers and bottled at no less than 40% ABV.

Straight rye must be aged at least two years. If it is under four years old the label must state its age. American rye can carry the words bottled in bond too, as our guide to straight bourbon and bottled in bond explains.

Many American ryes use far more than 51% rye. Some use close to 95%, with a little malted barley to supply enzymes. Others sit just over the line, with corn making up much of the rest.
Canadian rye can contain little rye

In Canada, the terms Canadian whisky, Canadian rye whisky and rye whisky are legally interchangeable. A whisky labelled Canadian rye does not have to contain any particular percentage of rye grain.

Canadian whisky must be mashed, distilled and aged in Canada, from cereal grains, for at least three years in small wood of no more than 700 litres. It must be bottled at no less than 40% ABV. It may contain caramel and flavouring. It may also contain up to 9.09% of other spirits or wine in the final blend.

The rye name is historical. Early Canadian distillers added rye to wheat mashes for flavour. The spicy result became known as rye whisky. The name stuck long after the recipes changed.

Most Canadian whisky is made by distilling each grain separately and blending afterwards. A common pattern is a base whisky, often from corn, distilled to a high strength for a light, clean spirit. A flavouring whisky, often from rye, is distilled to a lower strength to keep more character. The two are aged separately and blended to taste.

American rye usually ferments and distils the whole mash together. That difference in method is as important as the grain percentage. Our guide to Canadian whisky goes further into how blending works there.

American rye must go into new charred oak, every time. That gives strong vanilla, caramel and toasted wood notes. It gives them quickly.

Canadian whisky has no such rule. Distillers can use new barrels, used bourbon barrels or other casks. Many use a mix. Used barrels give a softer oak influence. Combined with a light corn base, that is why many Canadian whiskies feel smoother and gentler than a typical American rye.

Rye grain gives a recognisable set of flavours: black pepper, clove, dill, mint, rye bread and a dry, slightly bitter edge. Beer drinkers who have had a rye beer will know the spicy, bready note.

A high rye American whiskey puts those notes up front, wrapped in new oak vanilla and caramel. It is often bold, dry and spicy. A typical Canadian whisky is lighter, sweeter and smoother, with rye spice as an accent. Some Canadian whiskies are made with a high proportion of rye and taste every bit as spicy, so read beyond the word rye on the label.
Where rye sits in a cocktail

Rye whisky has a long history behind the bar. Classic drinks such as the Manhattan and the Sazerac were often made with rye. The grain's dry spice cuts through sweet vermouth and bitters in a way a soft whisky does not.

That is a practical way to taste the difference. Make two small, identical drinks, one with an American rye and one with a Canadian whisky, using the same measures, say 45 ml whisky to 20 ml vermouth. The American rye version will usually taste drier and spicier. The Canadian version will usually taste rounder and sweeter. If you want to judge the whiskies themselves, though, taste them neat first. A cocktail hides as much as it shows.
Tasting rye whisky in a warm room

Pour 20 ml of each into tulip glasses. Nose the American rye first and look for pepper and dill under the oak. Then nose the Canadian and see how much of that spice is left. Add a few drops of water to each and nose again.

In a warm Indian room the oak and alcohol jump out first. Let each glass sit for a minute, covered, before you judge. Drink water between pours, take small sips and never drink and drive.

Picking dill from mint or clove from pepper takes deliberate practice. Most tasters say spicy and stop there. Being able to say which spice is what separates a casual drinker from a trained taster.
Read the mash bill before the name

Your first step: next time you see the word rye on a bottle, find the country first. If it is American, rye is at least 51% of the grain. If it is Canadian, look for the producer's own statement of the rye content, because the label alone does not guarantee it. Then taste and see whether the spice matches the claim.
faqs: How much rye is in American rye whiskey?
At least 51% of the mash, by law. Many use much more.
Does Canadian rye whisky have to contain rye?
No. In Canada, rye whisky is a legal synonym for Canadian whisky and no minimum rye content is set.
How long must Canadian whisky be aged?
At least three years in small wood of no more than 700 litres, in Canada.
Why does rye whisky taste spicy?
Rye grain gives pepper, clove, dill and bready notes that carry through distillation, especially when it makes up most of the mash.
